body:
Maritime power under the Cholas

The Cholas were among the important maritime powers of early medieval southern India. Their position near the Bay of Bengal gave them access to sea routes connecting the Indian coast with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.

A navy is the maritime component of military power. It enables a kingdom to transport forces by sea, attack coastal targets and undertake operations beyond territories accessible by land.

During the reigns of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I, Chola power expanded through military campaigns on land and operations involving the sea.

Rajaraja I and the extension of Chola power

Rajaraja I expanded the Chola kingdom over neighbouring regions and conducted campaigns involving Sri Lanka.

These campaigns extended Chola influence beyond its original Kaveri delta heartland.

His son Rajendra I continued these policies and developed the maritime capability needed for major overseas expeditions.

Rajendra I's campaigns

Rajendra I is associated with 3 important geographical directions of expansion.

1. Northern expedition towards the Ganga

Rajendra I conducted a military expedition that reached the Ganga valley in northern India.

His victory was commemorated by the title Gangaikonda Chola and the establishment of Gangaikondacholapuram as a new imperial capital.

This expedition should be distinguished from the overseas naval campaigns. Reaching the Ganga valley did not mean that the entire northern region became a permanently administered part of the Chola heartland.

2. Campaigns involving Sri Lanka

Chola military operations also extended to Sri Lanka. Rajendra I continued the policies of his father in the region.

Sri Lanka lies across the sea from southern India and formed an important area of Chola military activity.

3. Naval expedition against Srivijaya

In 1025 CE, Rajendra I launched a major naval expedition against Srivijaya, a powerful maritime kingdom associated with Sumatra and important Southeast Asian ports.

The expedition involved attacks on Srivijayan-controlled centres and demonstrated the ability of the Cholas to send a substantial force across the Bay of Bengal.

Ports in this region occupied important positions along maritime trade routes linking South India with Southeast Asia and China.

What the naval expedition demonstrated

The expedition showed that Chola military power was not confined to land warfare. The kingdom could also organise ships, personnel and supplies for operations at considerable distances from its home territory.

The campaign is important for understanding the Cholas' connection with the wider maritime world of the Bay of Bengal.

However, a successful naval raid must not automatically be treated as permanent territorial annexation. The Srivijaya expedition is securely associated with Chola military action against overseas ports, but it should not be described as proof that all of Southeast Asia came under continuous Chola administration.

Distinguish the destinations

  • Ganga valley: Northern military expedition commemorated by Rajendra I.
  • Sri Lanka: Island region involved in Chola military campaigns.
  • Srivijaya: Southeast Asian maritime kingdom targeted by Rajendra I's naval expedition in 1025 CE.

Prelims focus

  • Rajaraja I expanded Chola authority through major military campaigns.
  • Rajendra I continued Chola operations involving Sri Lanka.
  • Rajendra I conducted a successful expedition towards the Ganga valley.
  • The major Chola naval expedition against Srivijaya took place in 1025 CE.
  • Srivijaya was associated with Southeast Asia, especially Sumatra and important maritime ports.
  • Trap: The expedition against Srivijaya was a naval raid, not evidence of permanent Chola administration over all Southeast Asian territories.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7 History, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, pp. 22-23; Hermann Kulke, The Naval Expeditions of the Cholas in the Context of Asian History, in Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa, Chapter 1 summary, Cambridge Core, consulted 18 November 2026; Tansen Sen, The Military Campaigns of Rajendra Chola and the Chola-Srivijaya-China Triangle, in Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa, Chapter 3 summary, Cambridge Core, consulted 18 November 2026; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, Naval War College and the Chola Building, Release ID 2010660, section The Chola Building, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Chola naval activity across the Bay of Bengal.

title: The Chola Navy and Rajendra I's Overseas Expeditions

body:
Royal temple construction under the Cholas

The Chola rulers were major patrons of temple architecture. Their most important surviving monuments include large stone temples constructed in the Dravida style of South Indian architecture.

Two especially important examples are the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur and the Brihadisvara Temple at Gangaikondacholapuram.

Both are associated with the worship of Shiva. They also demonstrate the connection between royal patronage, monumental construction and the cultural importance of temple towns.

Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur

The Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur was built by Rajaraja I and completed and consecrated around 1009-1010 CE.

The temple is also known as Brihadeshwara, Rajarajeswara or Rajarajesvaram.

It is a monumental stone temple dedicated to Shiva. Its most striking architectural feature is its exceptionally tall, stepped, pyramidal vimana, the tower rising over the principal shrine.

The temple complex contains sculptural decoration and inscriptions, and its scale reflects the resources available to the Chola monarchy.

The temple at Gangaikondacholapuram

The great Shiva temple at Gangaikondacholapuram was built by Rajendra I and completed around 1035 CE.

Rajendra I established Gangaikondacholapuram as a new capital to commemorate his successful expedition towards the Ganga.

The temple followed the broad Dravida architectural tradition seen at Thanjavur, but its main tower has a different visual character.

Compared with the more straight-sided and sharply rising tower at Thanjavur, the Gangaikondacholapuram vimana has a gentler upward curvature and recessed corners.

The temple is also known for its elaborate stone sculptures.

Comparison of the 2 major temples

FeatureThanjavurGangaikondacholapuram
Royal patronRajaraja IRajendra I
Approximate completion1009-1010 CE1035 CE
LocationThanjavur, Tamil NaduGangaikondacholapuram, Tamil Nadu
Principal dedicationShivaShiva
VimanaVery tall, monumental and relatively straight-sidedMore gently curving, with recessed corners
Historical associationRajaraja I's royal and architectural achievementsRajendra I's new capital and Ganga victory

Recognising the Dravida temple style

The 2 temples are important examples of South Indian Dravida architecture.

  • Garbhagriha: The innermost sanctum containing the principal deity.
  • Vimana: The tower above the principal sanctum, characteristically rising in stepped levels in Dravida architecture.
  • Gopuram: A gateway tower providing entrance through the temple enclosure.
  • Mandapa: A pillared hall forming part of the temple complex.

South Indian temples generally developed within enclosed compounds. Temple tanks and subsidiary shrines were also common features of the wider Dravida tradition.

Vimana and gopuram are not the same. The vimana rises above the principal shrine, while the gopuram marks an entrance to the temple enclosure.

Temples as economic and cultural centres

Chola temples were more than places of worship. They often became centres around which settlements developed.

Rulers and other donors granted land to temples. The agricultural produce and revenue associated with these endowments supported temple activities and the people employed there.

Temple-associated occupations included priests, cooks, garland makers, musicians, dancers, cleaners and various craftspeople.

Temples therefore contributed to religious, economic, social and cultural life. They also supported artistic production, including the manufacture of bronze images.

Prelims focus

  • Rajaraja I: Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur, around 1009-1010 CE.
  • Rajendra I: Shiva temple at Gangaikondacholapuram, around 1035 CE.
  • Both temples belong to the Dravida tradition of South Indian temple architecture.
  • The vimana rises above the sanctum; the gopuram is an entrance gateway.
  • Chola temples functioned as centres of worship, craft production and economic activity.
  • Trap: Gangaikondacholapuram was associated with Rajendra I, not Rajaraja I.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7 History, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, pp. 23-24; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, pp. 81-85; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Living Chola Temples, Brief Synthesis and Outstanding Universal Value, consulted 18 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Great Living Chola Temples, monument descriptions, consulted 18 November 2026; Government of Tamil Nadu, Ariyalur District, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, historical description, consulted 18 November 2026.]

body:
The importance of Chola bronzes

The Chola period witnessed remarkable achievements in metal sculpture, particularly during the 10th-12th centuries CE.

Bronze images were an important artistic tradition associated with South Indian temples. Most represented religious deities, although images of devotees were also produced.

These sculptures combined skilled metal casting with carefully modelled human forms, balanced postures and detailed ornamentation.

Unlike the massive stone temples constructed at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram, bronze sculptures were separate metal objects that could serve religious and ceremonial purposes.

The lost-wax method of bronze casting

One of the important techniques used for making bronze images was the lost-wax process, also known as cire perdue.

This technique allowed craftspeople to create detailed three-dimensional metal images.

Main stages of the process

  1. Making the wax model: The craftsperson prepared a wax representation of the required image, including its main form and details.
  2. Preparing the mould: The wax model was enclosed in a suitable clay-based mould, with arrangements for the movement of molten material.
  3. Removing the wax: Heating caused the wax to melt and escape, leaving a cavity corresponding to the original model.
  4. Pouring molten metal: Molten metal was introduced into the cavity and allowed to solidify.
  5. Finishing the sculpture: The mould was removed and the metal image was cleaned and finished.

The defining principle is that the wax model is removed during casting, leaving the space into which metal flows.

Bronze is principally a copper-based alloy. Historical image-casting traditions used different metal compositions, so every Chola-period metal image should not be assumed to have exactly the same alloy.

Shiva as Nataraja

The most widely recognised form associated with Chola bronze sculpture is Nataraja, representing Shiva in a dancing posture.

The Nataraja image combines movement with balance. The figure is commonly shown with multiple arms, one leg supporting the body and the other raised.

Important identifying features include:

  • Raised drum: A small drum, or damaru, held in an upper hand.
  • Flame: Fire held in another upper hand.
  • Gesture of reassurance: A hand displaying the abhaya gesture, associated with protection or freedom from fear.
  • Raised leg: An important feature of the dancing posture.
  • Apasmara: The dwarf figure beneath the supporting foot, representing ignorance or forgetfulness.
  • Circle of flames: A surrounding ring often framing the dancing figure.

Why bronze sculpture was connected with temples

Temple patronage encouraged the production of bronze images. Temples required skilled craftspeople, and their resources could support specialised artistic work.

The temple-centred economy therefore helped sustain sculpture, music, dance and other cultural activities.

Stone temples and bronze images were different artistic forms, but both reveal the importance of religious patronage and craftsmanship under the Cholas.

Chola temple architecture: Monumental stone buildings, especially at Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram.

Chola bronze sculpture: Cast metal images, especially the dancing Shiva or Nataraja, produced using skilled metalworking techniques.

Prelims focus

  • Chola bronze sculpture flourished particularly during the 10th-12th centuries CE.
  • The lost-wax process was an important technique for casting metal images.
  • Nataraja represents Shiva in a dancing posture.
  • Important Nataraja attributes include the damaru, flame, raised leg and circle of flames.
  • Apasmara, beneath the supporting foot, represents ignorance or forgetfulness.
  • Trap: The lost-wax process is a method of metal casting, not a technique for carving stone sculptures.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 7, Indian Bronze Sculpture, pp. 103-108, especially pp. 107-108 and the section The Lost-wax Process; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7 History, Chapter 2, New Kings and Kingdoms, p. 24; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Great Living Chola Temples, Brief Synthesis, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO, Great Living Chola Temples, Associated Living Heritage, updated 15 November 2024, consulted 18 November 2026.]
